<div class="ltx_page_content">

# DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models

<div class="ltx_authors">

<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Sean Man<sup>∗</sup> </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Gilad Deutch<sup>∗</sup> </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Roy Ganz </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Roi Ronen </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Shahar Tsiper </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Shai Mazor </span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Niv Nayman </span></span>

</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract">

###### Abstract

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is a fundamental task for digitizing
information, serving as a critical bridge between visual data and
textual understanding. While modern Vision-Language Models (VLM) have
achieved high accuracy in this domain, they predominantly rely on
autoregressive decoding, which becomes computationally expensive and
slow for long documents as it requires a sequential forward pass for
every generated token. We identify a key opportunity to overcome this
bottleneck: unlike open-ended generation, OCR is a highly deterministic
task where the visual input strictly dictates a unique output sequence,
theoretically enabling efficient, parallel decoding via diffusion
models. However, we show that existing masked diffusion models fail to
harness this potential; those introduce structural instabilities that
are benign in flexible tasks, like captioning, but catastrophic for the
rigid, exact-match requirements of OCR. To bridge this gap, we introduce
<span class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DODO</span>, the first VLM to
utilize block discrete diffusion and unlock its speedup potential for
OCR. By decomposing generation into blocks, DODO mitigates the
synchronization errors of global diffusion. Empirically, our method
achieves near state-of-the-art accuracy while enabling up to $`5\times`$
faster inference compared to autoregressive baselines.

</div>

<div class="ltx_keywords">

Diffusion Models, OCR, Vision-Language Models, Document Understanding

</div>

<div id="S1" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="2602.16872v2/x1.png" id="S1.F1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" width="747"
height="701" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.9.4.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span
id="S1.F1.6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span
id="S1.F1.6.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DODO: High-throughput
parallel generation.</span> Unlike autoregressive models constrained to
a strict left-to-right sequence, DODO generates text across the entire
canvas simultaneously (with same color) based on visual confidence. In
this example, it resolves <span class="math inline">148</span> tokens in
just <span class="math inline">20</span> forward passes (<span
class="math inline"> ≈ 7</span> tokens/step on average). Simultaneously
generated tokens are adaptively distributed across
steps.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Optical character recognition (OCR) is a core component of modern
document understanding systems, enabling the extraction of structured
text from images such as scanned documents, forms, and natural scenes.
Vision–language models are increasingly used for large-scale document
parsing and multimodal reasoning (Alayrac et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib4" class="ltx_ref">2022</a>; Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib21" class="ltx_ref">2022</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib22" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>; Ganz et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib18" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>; Dai et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib17" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>; Wu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib50" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>; Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib20" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>; Ganz et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib19" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>; Chen et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>; Bai et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib9" class="ltx_ref">a</a>; Liu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib28" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>). However, the high
computational cost and latency of these architectures have
re-established OCR transcription as a critical bottleneck where both
accuracy and inference efficiency are essential (Blecher et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib12" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>; Wei et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib45" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>; Abramovich et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib3" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>; Nacson et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib32" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>; Wei et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib47" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>).

</div>

<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">

Crucially, OCR differs fundamentally from semantically flexible tasks
like image captioning (Sidorov et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib41" class="ltx_ref">2020</a>; Chen et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib13" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>; Lin et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib26" class="ltx_ref">2014</a>) or visual question
answering (VQA) (Antol et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib5" class="ltx_ref">2015</a>; Singh et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib42" class="ltx_ref">2019</a>; Mathew et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib31" class="ltx_ref">2021</a>; Yue et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib53" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>) as it is semantically
rigid. Conditioned on the image, the posterior distribution is
effectively unimodal, meaning the visual input strictly dictates a
single valid sequence. This determinism exposes a critical inefficiency
in standard Autoregressive (AR) models: they generate text sequentially,
creating a significant latency bottleneck for long document sequences.
Conversely, this characteristic makes OCR uniquely suited for Masked
Diffusion Models (MDMs) (Sahoo et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib39" class="ltx_ref">2024b</a>). Because the output
allows for little ambiguity, OCR satisfies the MDM assumption of
<span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">conditional
independence</span>—the premise that tokens can be predicted
independently given the input (Azangulov et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib8" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>). Theoretically, this
allows the model to resolve large spans of text simultaneously, similar
to how traditional OCR pipelines (Wang et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib44" class="ltx_ref">2021</a>; Ronen et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib37" class="ltx_ref">2022</a>; Aberdam et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib2" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>) recognize isolated regions
in parallel without the risk of incoherence.

</div>

<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">

However, realizing this potential in practice reveals a structural
paradox: the same rigidity that enables parallelization also makes OCR
particularly sensitive to the instabilities of global decoding. While
standard MDMs (Yu et al., <a href="#bib.bib52" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>;
Li et al., <a href="#bib.bib23" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>; You et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib51" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>) can generate tokens in
parallel, they introduce non-causal structural uncertainties,
specifically regarding sequence length and absolute positional
alignment. In flexible tasks like captioning, such errors are
recoverable: the model can navigate a wide space of valid outputs to
resolve a misalignment dynamically. OCR allows no such flexibility.
Because the target is a single, immutable sequence, structural errors
become irrecoverable; the model cannot “rewrite” the text to compensate
for incorrect length estimates or token placement. Consequently, these
rigidities force the model to either truncate valid text or hallucinate
padding, leading to fractured, colliding outputs that fundamentally
undermine the efficacy of standard masked diffusion for transcription.

</div>

<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">

To resolve this paradox, we propose DODO (<span id="S1.p4.2.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_underline">D</span>iscrete
<span id="S1.p4.2.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_underline">O</span>CR
<span id="S1.p4.2.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_underline">D</span>iffusion
M<span id="S1.p4.2.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_underline">o</span>dels), the
first Vision–Language Model to adapt block discrete diffusion for
document transcription. Unlike standard global diffusion, DODO
decomposes the monolithic generation task into a sequence of causally
anchored blocks. This structural change directly addresses the
rigidities of OCR: by bounding the inference horizon and conditioning on
a committed prefix, we eliminate the risk of long-range alignment drift
and enable dynamic length adaptation without requiring a perfect global
estimate. Crucially, we leverage the high-confidence nature of OCR
combined with block-causal attention and KV-caching (Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib20" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>) to achieve both causal
consistency and fast inference. Moreover, unlike autoregressive models,
the diffusion framework uniquely enables bidirectional attention across
blocks, which we show pushes the utilizable block size from $`32`$ to
$`256`$ tokens, further improving accuracy.

</div>

<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">

Empirically, DODO achieves transcription accuracy competitive with
state-of-the-art autoregressive models while outperforming the
equivalent autoregressive baseline in throughput. These results validate
our hypothesis: OCR is indeed a regime where the conditional
independence assumption holds, but it requires the structural safety
rails of block diffusion to be realized in practice. Appropriately
structured, DODO recovers the correctness of AR models while unlocking
the efficiency benefits that motivate diffusion-based decoding in the
first place.

</div>

<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- <span id="S1.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  We identify a structural incompatibility between standard masked
  diffusion and the rigid requirements of OCR, explaining why positional
  and length errors that are benign in flexible tasks prove catastrophic
  for OCR.

  </div>
- <span id="S1.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  We introduce <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1"
  class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DODO</span>, the first VLM to utilize
  block discrete diffusion. By decomposing generation into sequentially
  conditioned blocks, DODO enforces local alignment and enables dynamic
  length adaptation, resolving the rigidities of global diffusion.

  </div>
- <span id="S1.I1.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  We demonstrate that DODO matches the accuracy of state-of-the-art
  autoregressive baselines while enabling up to $`5\times`$ faster
  inference, validating the potential of parallel decoding for dense
  text recognition.

  </div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work

<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="2602.16872v2/x2.png" id="S2.F2.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="135" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.5.1.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span
id="S2.F2.6.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span
id="S2.F2.6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Semantically flexible
<em>vs</em>.<span id="S2.F2.6.2.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>
semantically rigid vision–language tasks.</span> <span id="S2.F2.6.2.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Left:</span> Image captioning admits
multiple, semantically equivalent descriptions of the same image.
Different decoding trajectories can converge to distinct but equally
valid captions, and lexical or structural variations are naturally
absorbed. <span id="S2.F2.6.2.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Right:</span> OCR requires a single,
exact transcription determined by the image. Even minimal local
deviations, such as an incorrect token choice or boundary, render the
output incorrect. As a result, conditioned on the image, OCR exhibits
extremely low output variability, which makes it a natural candidate for
parallel decoding, but also a demanding setting in which errors cannot
be compensated by alternative phrasings or later corrections.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Specialized OCR and Document Understanding.

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Modern OCR systems leverage vision-language models for end-to-end
document understanding. MonkeyOCR (Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib25" class="ltx_ref">2025c</a>) introduces a multi-stage
pipeline with detection, recognition, and reading order prediction.
MinerU (Wang et al., <a href="#bib.bib43" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>) and
commercial systems like dots.ocr (Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib24" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>), DeepSeek-OCR (Wei
et al., <a href="#bib.bib46" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>),
Mistral-OCR (mis, <a href="#bib.bib1" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>) achieve
strong performance through careful engineering and large-scale training.
These methods universally employ autoregressive decoding. This is the
first successful attempt to achieve competitive OCR performance by MDMs.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Discrete Diffusion Models.

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Discrete diffusion models learn to reverse a corruption process over
discrete tokens. D3PM (Austin et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib7" class="ltx_ref">2021</a>) introduced structured
transition matrices, while MDLM (Sahoo et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib38" class="ltx_ref">2024a</a>) simplified training
through masked diffusion with a tighter evidence lower bounds (ELBO).
Recent work has scaled these models to language modeling (Zhou et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib55" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>), though a gap remains
compared to autoregressive models on perplexity benchmarks. This work
narrows down the performance gap of MDMs with their plain autoregressive
counterparts for the studied task.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Block Diffusion.

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

Block Diffusion (BD3-LM) (Arriola et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib6" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>) bridges autoregressive and
diffusion models by generating blocks of tokens autoregressively during
inference only, with each block decoded via masked diffusion. This
enables KV-caching across blocks while maintaining parallel decoding
within blocks. Prior work uses small block sizes (4–32 tokens) (Wu
et al., <a href="#bib.bib49" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>) to minimize the
performance gap with autoregressive models on language modeling. (Wu
et al., <a href="#bib.bib48" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>) further aligns
the attention masks to be block causal during training. We implement
this approach for VLMs.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Multimodal Diffusion Models.

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">

Dimple (Yu et al., <a href="#bib.bib52" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>)
extends discrete diffusion to vision-language tasks, training on the
LLaVA recipe. However, it shows limited gains over autoregressive
baselines and does not evaluate on OCR benchmarks. LaViDa (Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib23" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>) and LLaDA-V (You et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib51" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>) explore diffusion for VQA
but struggle with OCR tasks requiring precise text reproduction. This
work is the first to successfully apply discrete diffusion for OCR.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Preliminaries

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Notation.

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Let $`\mathcal{V}`$ be a vocabulary of size $`V`$, and let
$`\mathtt{[M]}\notin\mathcal{V}`$ denote a dedicated
<span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.8.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MASK</span> token. We write
$`\tilde{\mathcal{V}}=\mathcal{V}\cup\{\mathtt{[M]}\}`$, and represent
tokens either as categorical indices $`v\in\tilde{\mathcal{V}}`$ or as
one-hot vectors $`\mathbf{e}_{v}\in\{0,1\}^{|\tilde{\mathcal{V}}|}`$. We
use $`\mathrm{Cat}(\cdot;\pi)`$ for a categorical distribution with
probabilities $`\pi`$.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>OCR as Conditional Sequence Modeling

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We formulate OCR as a conditional generation task where the goal is to
map a document image $`I`$ to a target sequence of discrete tokens
$`x^{1:L}`$. This target is defined as $`x^{1:L}=\tau(s(I))`$, where
$`s(\cdot)`$ represents a fixed serialization scheme (e.g., plain text,
<span id="S3.SS1.p1.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_LaTeX_logo"
style="letter-spacing:-0.2em; margin-right:0.1em;">L<span id="S3.SS1.p1.8.1.1"
class="ltx_text"
style="position:relative; bottom:0.4ex;font-variant:small-caps;;">a</span>T<span class="smallcaps">e</span>X</span>,
HTML) and $`\tau(\cdot)`$ is a tokenizer that maps the resulting string
to vocabulary indices. A vision–language model (VLM) estimates the
conditional distribution $`p_{\theta}(x^{1:L}\mid I,c)`$ given the image
$`I`$ and optional text context $`c`$. Autoregressive (AR) VLM decoding
admits standard left-to-right factorization

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
\log p_{\theta}(x^{1:L}\mid I,c)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\log p_{\theta}(x^{\ell}\mid x^{<\ell},I,c),
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span> |

with $`x^{<l}`$ the prefix tokens at step $`l`$ out of $`L`$ sequential
steps.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs)

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Forward (Masking) Process.

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

MDMs define a coordinate-independent corruption process that replaces
tokens with $`\mathtt{[M]}`$ according to a noise level $`t\in[0,1]`$.
Writing $`x_{0}`$ for clean data and $`x_{t}`$ for its noisy version, a
common conditional probability distribution for the token masking is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
q_{t|0}(x_{t}\mid x_{0})=\prod_{i=1}^{L}\mathrm{Cat}\!\Big(x_{t}^{i};\ \alpha_{t}\,\mathbf{e}_{x_{0}^{i}}+(1-\alpha_{t})\,\mathbf{e}_{\mathtt{[M]}}\Big),
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span> |

where $`\alpha_{t}`$ is strictly decreasing with $`\alpha_{0}\!=\!1`$
and $`\alpha_{1}\!=\!0`$.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Training.

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

MDMs train a denoiser to predict the original input tokens from
partially masked ones. In continuous time, an ELBO-derived objective can
be written (Sahoo et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib38" class="ltx_ref">2024a</a>; Shi et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib40" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>) as a weighted masked
cross-entropy

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_{0},x_{t}|x_{0}}\left[\frac{\alpha^{\prime}_{t}}{1-\alpha_{t}}\sum_{i:x_{t}^{i}=\texttt{[M]}}-\log p_{\theta}(x_{0}^{i}|x_{t},t)\right],
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span> |

where $`\alpha^{\prime}_{t}=\frac{d\alpha_{t}}{dt}`$, and
$`p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t},t)`$ is frequently implemented without an
explicit time embedding since $`x_{t}`$ reveals $`t`$ through its mask
rate.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Sampling.

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

MDM sampling starts from the fully masked sequence
$`x_{1}=(\mathtt{[M]},\dots,\mathtt{[M]})`$ and iterates noise levels
$`1=t_{K}>\cdots>t_{0}=0`$. Given an estimate of the marginal
distribution of each token from the denoiser, a common and convenient
decomposition (Sahoo et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib38" class="ltx_ref">2024a</a>) of a single reverse step
$`t_{k+1}\to t_{k}`$ proceeds by *first* choosing which masked positions
to reveal via a selection rule (e.g., randomly (Sahoo et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib38" class="ltx_ref">2024a</a>), top-k (Zheng et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib54" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>),
confidence-thresholding (Yu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib52" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>), or
deterministically (Luxembourg et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib29" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>)), and *second*, sampling
token values for those positions from the denoiser’s predicted
distribution
$`x_{t_{k}}^{i}\sim p_{\theta}(x_{t_{k}}^{i}\mid x_{t_{k+1}})`$.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">

This decomposition has two consequences described next.

</div>

<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="2602.16872v2/x3.png" id="S3.F3.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="304" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.5.1.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span
id="S3.F3.6.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span
id="S3.F3.6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conditional independence
assumption.</span> <em>(Top)</em> In open-ended tasks, ambiguity between
valid options risks sampling incoherent mixtures. <em>(Bottom)</em> In
OCR, the strong visual signal resolves this ambiguity, enabling
conflict-free parallel decoding. </span></figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Conditional Independence Assumption.

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">

At each sampling step, the decoded tokens are sampled independently from
one another. This may lead to incorrect results if the decoded tokens in
fact are conditionally dependent given the context, as illustrated in
<a href="#S3.F3" class="ltx_ref"
title="In Sampling. ‣ 3.2 Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. On the other hand, when this
assumption holds, there is a large parallelization potential to
leverage.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Carry-Over Unmasking.

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">

We follow the common practice (Wu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib49" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib48" class="ltx_ref">a</a>; You et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib51" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>; Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib23" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>; Yu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib52" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>) and only allow the
sampling of masked tokens at each step. While this formulation is shown
by (Sahoo et al., <a href="#bib.bib38" class="ltx_ref">2024a</a>) to be
the key for the derivation of the discrete ELBO equivalent loss in
<a href="#S3.E1" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 3.1 OCR as Conditional Sequence Modeling ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, this means one cannot revise
previously decoded tokens. While this has a lesser effect on generative
tasks where multiple responses are acceptable, it might be detrimental
for tasks where only one response is correct, as illustrated in
<a href="#S2.F2" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 2 Related Work ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.

</div>

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Method

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">

We analyze OCR through the lens of MDM training and sampling
(<a href="#S3.SS2" class="ltx_ref"
title="3.2 Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>), focusing on the two
sampling assumptions made explicit there: *conditional independence* of
tokens sampled within a step, and *carry-over unmasking*, where revealed
tokens are not revised.

</div>

<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">

We first argue that OCR is especially compatible with the
conditional-independence assumption. We then show why this potential is
difficult to realize with vanilla MDM inference, as early mistakes
persist and this requires caution when decoding many tokens in parallel.
Finally, we argue that block discrete diffusion mitigates these failure
modes, while retaining high parallelism and enjoying KV-Caching.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Parallel Decoding Potential

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

OCR typically yields long sequences, making standard autoregressive
decoding a significant latency bottleneck, as it requires $`L`$
sequential forward passes to decode $`L`$ tokens. Masked diffusion
models offer a compelling alternative by enabling parallel token
generation; however, their effectiveness hinges on the validity of the
*conditional independence assumption*.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

We argue that OCR is uniquely suited for this parallel paradigm. Unlike
semantically flexible vision-language tasks, the posterior distribution
$`p(x^{1:L}|I,c)`$ for document transcription is highly peaked, often
approaching a Dirac delta function around a single ground-truth
sequence. In this low-entropy regime, the strong conditioning on the
visual input effectively decouples token predictions, allowing the joint
probability of masked tokens to be factorized:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
p(x^{1:L}_{t_{k}}\mid x^{1:L}_{t_{k+1}},I,c)\approx\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}p(x^{\ell}_{t_{k}}\mid x^{1:L}_{t_{k+1}},I,c).
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span> |

This independence allows the decoding of large spans of tokens
simultaneously, as shown in <a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 1 Introduction ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Brittleness of Parallel Decoding in OCR

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Standard masked diffusion models operate on a fixed-length canvas and
rely on *carry-over unmasking*
(<a href="#S3.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Carry-Over Unmasking. ‣ 3.2 Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>), treating tokens revealed
in early steps as immutable context. While this constraint is manageable
for semantically flexible tasks like captioning, where the model can
paraphrase content or alter semantics to fit the available space, it
presents a fundamental challenge for OCR. Document transcription is a
rigid, zero-tolerance task: the ground-truth text consists of a specific
set of characters in an immutable order. This lack of flexibility
exposes two critical failure modes for parallel decoding:

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Length Mismatch.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Because the true sequence length is unknown at inference time, the
decoding canvas size is effectively an estimate. In generative tasks
like captioning, this is rarely fatal; the model can simply generate a
valid shorter or longer description to match the canvas. In OCR,
however, this mismatch creates a structural vulnerability. If the
initial $`L`$ is incorrect, or the model predicts an end-of-sequence
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">\[EOS\]</span> token prematurely,
the model is forced to either truncate valid text (if the effective
length is too short) or hallucinate (if too long) to satisfy the imposed
constraint.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Positional Anchoring.

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Even with a valid length estimate, parallel decoding binds content to
absolute positional indices in a non-causal manner. This introduces a
critical synchronization risk: the model may predict a segment at an
incorrect offset, such as placing a table header $`50`$ tokens too early
or too late. Because *carry-over unmasking* prevents the revision of
revealed tokens, this error is locked in place. Unlike autoregressive
decoding, which inherently align content to its history without looking
ahead, diffusion parallel decoding is bound to errors made ahead.
Consequently, the subsequent text cannot shift to accommodate the
offset. Due to the unimodal nature of OCR, the model cannot simply
paraphrase or “tweak” the surrounding text to bridge this misalignment,
leading to fractured outputs where disjoint segments collide – a
fundamental challenge that limits the efficacy of purely parallel OCR.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Block Diffusion as a Structural Remedy

<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="2602.16872v2/x4.png" id="S4.F4.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="344" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.5.1.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span
id="S4.F4.6.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span
id="S4.F4.6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Full <em>vs</em>.<span
id="S4.F4.6.2.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span> block diffusion</span>. In
standard full diffusion (<em>left</em>), MDM sampling is applied
globally to the entire sequence. In contrast, block diffusion
(<em>right</em>) restricts parallel sampling to discrete windows,
processing blocks sequentially from left to right. </span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

Block discrete diffusion can mitigate these failure modes by replacing a
single length-$`L`$ denoising problem with a sequence of bounded-span
problems, conditioned of a prefix composed on previous blocks decoded
sequentially.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">

Block discrete diffusion models (Arriola et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib6" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>) combine AR structure at a
coarse granularity with diffusion within blocks. Partition the sequence
into $`B`$ contiguous blocks of length $`L^{\prime}`$ (so
$`L=BL^{\prime}`$) and write $`x^{(b)}`$ for block $`b`$ and
$`x^{(<b)}`$ for the prefix blocks. The model factorizes as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | 
``` math
p_{\theta}(x^{1:L}|I,c)=\prod_{b=1}^{B}p_{\theta}\!\big(x^{(b)}\mid x^{(<b)},I,c\big),
``` |  | <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span> |

where each conditional distribution
$`p_{\theta}(x^{(b)}\mid x^{(<b)},I,c)`$ is implemented via a masked
diffusion sampling over the $`L^{\prime}`$ tokens of the block,
conditioned on prefix states. This formulation narrows the performance
gap between MDMs and AR models and enables significant computational
efficiency by allowing the KV-cache of committed prefix blocks
$`x^{(<b)}`$ to be reused rather than recomputed. An illustrative
example of the difference between full and block diffusion models
sampling is given in <a href="#S4.F4" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 4.3 Block Diffusion as a Structural Remedy ‣ 4 Method ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. This factorization anchors
indices and conventions at block boundaries, reduces length sensitivity,
and retains parallel token updates within each block while enabling
variable-length generation via block-level stopping.

</div>

<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">

Previous unimodal MDMs (Wu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib49" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>,
<a href="#bib.bib48" class="ltx_ref">a</a>) use small block sizes (4–32
tokens) to minimize the performance gap with autoregressive models on
text-only tasks. By utilizing the properties of the OCR task and
equipping the model with bidirectional attention across blocks, we are
able to scale the block size from $`32`$ to $`256`$ tokens. Finally,
this work is the first to apply block-causal masking both during
training and inference in the multimodal VLM settings.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments

<div id="S5.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>DODO

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We instantiate our proposed framework as <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DODO</span> (<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_underline">D</span>iscrete
<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.3"
class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_underline">O</span>CR
<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.4"
class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_underline">D</span>iffusion
M<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.5"
class="ltx_text ltx_framed ltx_framed_underline">o</span>dels), built
upon the Qwen2.5-VL-3B architecture (Bai et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref">2025c</a>). We train DODO on
<span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.6"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">olmOCR-mix-1025</span> (Poznanski
et al., <a href="#bib.bib35" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>), a large-scale
OCR dataset comprising approximately 270K document-text pairs derived
from PDFs. The dataset covers diverse document types, including academic
papers, books, reports, and web pages, with text extracted using a
combination of PDF parsing and OCR pipelines. While block-based
diffusion has previously been explored for text-only models (Arriola
et al., <a href="#bib.bib6" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>; Wu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib48" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>), we are the first to
adapt this paradigm to the multimodal domain.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

DODO employs a *block-causal* attention mask: tokens within the active
block $`x^{(b)}`$ attend bidirectionally to one another and to all
previous blocks $`x^{(<b)}`$, but attention from previous blocks to the
current one is masked. This strict causality ensures that the
representations of the committed prefix remain fixed, enabling the use
of an exact Key-Value (KV) cache. Consequently, only the active block
needs to be computed at each step, resulting in significant speedups.
Furthermore, unlike autoregressive models, the diffusion framework also
permits full bidirectional attention across blocks, which we show in
<a href="#S6.SS1" class="ltx_ref"
title="6.1 Vanilla vs. Block Training ‣ 6 Ablation and Empirical Analysis ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a> can further improve accuracy
by enabling larger effective block sizes.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Implementation Details

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

We fine-tune the model with a maximum sequence length of $`8192`$ tokens
to accommodate dense document texts, retaining the default image
preprocessing pipeline. A visualization of the attention structure is
provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix A Attention Structure Visualization ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Training Configuration.

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We train DODO for a total of $`200,000`$ steps on a node of
$`8\times`$NVIDIA A100 (40GB) GPUs, using a global batch size of $`8`$.
Optimization is performed using AdamW with a peak learning rate of
$`5\times 10^{-6}`$ and a weight decay of $`0.01`$. We employ a
Warmup-Steady-Decay (WSD) learning rate scheduler, consisting of a
linear warmup for $`5,000`$ steps, a constant steady phase, and a linear
cooldown to zero over the final $`20,000`$ steps. To ensure training
stability and efficiency, we utilize <span id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.7.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">bfloat16</span> precision
throughout the process.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Diffusion Setup.

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Following recent advances in discrete diffusion (Wu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib48" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>; Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib23" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>), we utilize
complementary masking during training. For timestep sampling, we employ
stratified uniform scheduling to ensure balanced coverage of the noise
levels during training.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Evaluation Setup

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Benchmarks.

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate our models on two distinct benchmarks. First, we use
<span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">OmniDocBench</span> (Ouyang et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>), a comprehensive testbed
for layout-sensitive transcription containing 290 English documents
across 9 diverse types (e.g., academic papers, financial reports),
annotated with structured ground truth for text, tables, and formulas.
Second, we evaluate on <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Fox-Page-EN</span> (Liu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib27" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>), a dataset of 112
document pages focused exclusively on pure text without figures or
tables. This combination allows us to assess performance on both
complex, multimodal document layouts and standard dense text
transcription.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Metrics.

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">

We assess performance using two metrics. First, we report accuracy using
the Normalized Edit Distance (NED) between the predicted and
ground-truth text, with lower scores indicating higher fidelity. Second,
to quantify inference efficiency, we measure throughput as the number of
generated Tokens Per Second (TPS) for each model.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Baselines.

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">

We compare DODO against three model categories: (1) specialized OCR
models, including dots.ocr, DeepSeek-OCR, MinerU 2.0 VLM, MonkeyOCR,
MistralOCR, olmOCR, Nanonets-OCR-s, and SmolDocling (Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib24" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>; Wei et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib46" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>; Wang et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib43" class="ltx_ref">2024</a>; Li et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib25" class="ltx_ref">2025c</a>; mis,
<a href="#bib.bib1" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>; Poznanski et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib36" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>; Mandal et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib30" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>; Nassar et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib33" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>); (2) general-purpose
autoregressive VLMs, specifically the Qwen2.5-VL family (Bai et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref">2025c</a>), which serves as our
backbone; and (3) diffusion VLMs, represented by Dimple, LaViDa, and
LLaDA-V (Yu et al., <a href="#bib.bib52" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>; Li
et al., <a href="#bib.bib23" class="ltx_ref">2025a</a>; You et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib51" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>).

</div>

</div>

</div>

performance on the English subset of OmniDocBench and Fox-Pages. Bold
numbers indicate the best value across each model type (MDM and AR).
</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">

<a href="#S5.T1" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 5.4 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> presents the OCR performance
on OmniDocBench (breakdown by document length and type is provided in
Appendix <a href="#A3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix C Fine-Grained Evaluation Breakdown ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>) and Fox-Pages. Compared to
prior diffusion-based VLMs, DODO demonstrates a substantial performance
leap. Standard diffusion models such as Dimple, LaViDa, and LLaDA-V
struggle significantly with dense document transcription, incurring high
error rates ($`>0.5`$ NED on OmniDocBench). In contrast, DODO achieves
an NED of $`0.069`$. While DODO benefits from specialized OCR training,
we demonstrate in our ablations (<a href="#S6.SS1" class="ltx_ref"
title="6.1 Vanilla vs. Block Training ‣ 6 Ablation and Empirical Analysis ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a>) that data distribution
alone does not explain this gap; even when trained on identical OCR
data, standard full-sequence diffusion fails to converge on dense text.
This confirms that the improvement is primarily structural: DODO’s
block-wise constraints effectively mitigate the alignment failures that
plague global diffusion models.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">

Second, DODO proves highly competitive against strong autoregressive and
specialized baselines. On the layout-intensive OmniDocBench, it
surpasses its own autoregressive backbone, the Qwen2.5-VL family, across
all model scales. Furthermore, DODO outperforms various specialized
models and achieves near-parity with robust engines such as MonkeyOCR
(Li et al., <a href="#bib.bib25" class="ltx_ref">2025c</a>) and Mistral
OCR (mis, <a href="#bib.bib1" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>). These results
establish that discrete diffusion is a viable, high-performance
alternative to the dominant autoregressive paradigm in the challenging
domain of dense text recognition.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS5" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.5 </span>Throughput Analysis

<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="2602.16872v2/x5.png" id="S5.F5.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="472" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F5.7.3.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span
id="S5.F5.4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"
style="font-size:90%;">Inference throughput comparison.<span
id="S5.F5.4.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> DODO leverages
parallel decoding, block-causal attention and KV-caching to achieve
<span class="math inline"> ≈ 104</span> tokens/sec, a <span
class="math inline">5×</span> speedup over the autoregressive
baseline.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">

Figure <a href="#S5.F5" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.5 Throughput Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> illustrates the inference
throughput across different model architectures. For qualitative
visualizations of the parallel decoding process on dense documents, we
refer readers to <a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 1 Introduction ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and
<a href="#A4" class="ltx_ref"
title="Appendix D Document Parsing Examples ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>. Two key trends emerge from
this comparison.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">

First, DODO achieves $`\approx 105`$ tokens per second, a $`5\times`$
speedup over the autoregressive Qwen 2.5 VL baseline. For analysis
purposes alone, we isolate the contribution of parallel decoding to the
speedup, by running both the AR baseline and DODO+Bidir without
KV-caching. The speedup of parallel decoding alone is evaluated as
$`20\times`$ (42.8 vs. 2.2 TPS), demonstrating that a significant part
of the throughput gain stems from generating multiple tokens per step.
By enabling the use of an exact KV-cache for completed blocks, DODO
eliminates the redundant re-computation of prefix representations,
maximizing deployment efficiency. While AR generation requires $`L`$
sequential steps, DODO decouples latency from sequence length, allowing
parallel predictions of multiple tokens to amortize the cost of heavier
forward passes.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">

Second, DODO achieves significantly higher throughput than competing
diffusion VLMs. Prior methods rely on full-sequence attention from the
outset, incurring the maximal computational cost proportional to the
total length $`L`$ at every denoising step. In contrast, DODO combines
parallel decoding within blocks with constant cost per block by caching
the prefix, allowing it to process generation much faster than standard
diffusion baselines, which are immediately burdened by the full sequence
complexity.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S6" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Ablation and Empirical Analysis

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">

We validate the structural design of DODO by isolating the impact of
block-based training and analyzing the interaction between block size
and caching strategies. For an ablation of sampling schedules, we refer
readers to <a href="#A2.SS1" class="ltx_ref"
title="B.1 Sampling Strategies ‣ Appendix B Additional Ablations ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.

</div>

<div id="S6.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Vanilla *vs*.<span id="S6.SS1.2.2" class="ltx_text"></span> Block Training

id="S6.T2.5.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Impact of block
structure.</span> Vanilla MDM fails even with Oracle length; block-wise
<span id="S6.T2.5.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">training</span>
is essential. </span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

<a href="#S6.T2" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 6.1 Vanilla vs. Block Training ‣ 6 Ablation and Empirical Analysis ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> serves as the empirical
validation of the theoretical challenges outlined in
<a href="#S4" class="ltx_ref"
title="4 Method ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. We compare our block-based
approach against a “Vanilla” baseline: a standard masked diffusion model
trained on global sequences (up to 8192 tokens) without block
decomposition.

</div>

<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

The baseline model exhibits high error rates compared to DODO.
Crucially, this performance gap persists even when the model is provided
with the *oracle* sequence length. This suggests that the limitation is
not solely due to length estimation, but also stems from the positional
anchoring inherent to parallel decoding. Attempting to resolve thousands
of tokens simultaneously on a fixed canvas creates synchronization
risks; because the model cannot adjust the global offset of disjoint
text segments, the output becomes fractured.

</div>

<div id="S6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">

We further investigate if this issue can be mitigated solely at
inference time by applying block decoding to the baseline model. The
results show that restricting the decoding window without a
corresponding training objective leads to poor performance. This
contrasts with findings in fast-dLLM (Wu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib49" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>), where inference-time
blocking remained effective for math and coding benchmarks like
GSM8K (Cobbe et al., <a href="#bib.bib16" class="ltx_ref">2021</a>) and
HumanEval (Chen et al., <a href="#bib.bib14" class="ltx_ref">2021</a>).
We hypothesize that this divergence stems from the nature of the tasks,
as unlike OCR, they allow some semantic or syntactic flexibility. This
indicates that block diffusion serves as a necessary structural prior
for OCR, conditioning the model to treat the prefix $`x^{(<b)}`$ as a
stable anchor.

</div>

<div id="S6.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">

Finally, the baseline exhibits significantly lower throughput. This is
due to the computational cost of the global canvas: the model must
compute attention over the full sequence length (up to 8192 tokens) at
every denoising step. In contrast, DODO decomposes the workload,
ensuring a more efficient distribution of computational cost.

</div>

</div>

class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span
id="S6.T3.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span
id="S6.T3.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Block size and
caching.</span> Approx. KV-Cache collapses; block-causal training
enables exact caching with <span class="math inline">5×</span> speedup.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

Table <a href="#S6.T3" class="ltx_ref"
title="Table 3 ‣ 6.2 Block Size and Caching Strategies ‣ 6 Ablation and Empirical Analysis ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> investigates the impact of
block size and KV-caching strategies on performance. For the standard
bidirectional model (No KV-Cache), we observe a non-monotonic trend as
the block size increases. Initially, enlarging the block size improves
both throughput and accuracy, peaking at an intermediate size
($`B=256`$). This is because generating more tokens in parallel reduces
the total number of sequential inference steps, amortizing the cost of
the forward pass. However, further increasing the block size
($`B=512,1024`$) leads to diminishing returns in throughput and a
notable degradation in accuracy. We attribute this to the recurrence of
positional anchoring issues: as the block becomes sufficiently large, it
begins to suffer from the same internal synchronization failures that
plague the global canvas.

</div>

<div id="S6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

The “Approx. KV-Cache” configurations investigate the feasibility of
reusing computed keys and values in a bidirectional model without
retraining. Unlike prior findings which observed minimal degradation
when freezing history in standard diffusion models (Wu et al.,
<a href="#bib.bib49" class="ltx_ref">2025b</a>), our experiments show a
sharp accuracy collapse. We attribute this discrepancy to the rigid
nature of the OCR task.

</div>

<div id="S6.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">

DODO resolves this incompatibility by explicitly training with
block-causal masks, enabling exact KV-caching. However, the diffusion
framework offers an additional capability unavailable to autoregressive
models: bidirectional attention across blocks. Equipping it with
bidirectional attention allows the context to dynamically adapt to the
current active block by recomputing prefix representations at every
step. This reduces the risk of representation drift when generating
large blocks, effectively pushing the utilizable block size from $`32`$
to $`256`$ tokens and thus further improve accuracy. We observe that
while DODO performs best with smaller blocks ($`B=32`$), equipping it
with bidirectional attention uniquely scales to larger blocks
($`B=256`$), demonstrating that this is a powerful mechanism for
enhancing parallel decoding in diffusion models.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S6.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>Inference Efficiency Analysis

<figure id="S6.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="2602.16872v2/x6.png" id="S6.F6.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="830"
height="514" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F6.5.2.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span
id="S6.F6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"
style="font-size:90%;">Decoding Efficiency.<span id="S6.F6.2.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> DODO requires fewer than <span
class="math inline">0.1</span> steps per token, compressing inference by
an order of magnitude vs. autoregressive
models.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

To disentangle the source of DODO’s throughput advantage, we analyze the
number of model forward passes required for generation in
<a href="#S6.F6" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 6.3 Inference Efficiency Analysis ‣ 6 Ablation and Empirical Analysis ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. Autoregressive models are
structurally bound to a $`1:1`$ ratio (one step per token). In contrast,
DODO leverages parallel decoding to compress the inference process,
typically requiring fewer than $`0.1`$ steps per token. This
order-of-magnitude reduction in the number of sequential steps explains
the throughput results shown in <a href="#S5.F5" class="ltx_ref"
title="In 5.5 Throughput Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Although DODO’s bidirectional
forward pass (without caching) is computationally heavier than a cached
autoregressive step, the sheer reduction in the number of calls,
generating 10 to 20 tokens per AR step, overcomes the per-step cost.
This allows DODO to outperform optimized autoregressive baselines even
without KV caching.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S7" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">

In this work, we introduce DODO, a framework that unlocks the potential
of masked diffusion models to accelerate OCR via parallel decoding. Our
analysis reveals that standard parallel decoding is fundamentally
limited by the brittleness of the monolithic canvas, which leads to
catastrophic synchronization failures due to length mismatches and
positional anchoring. By decomposing this task into semi-autoregressive
blocks, DODO provides a structural remedy that reconciles the stability
of causal anchoring with the efficiency of parallel generation.
Empirically, DODO sets a new standard for non-autoregressive OCR VLMs.
It surpasses prior diffusion-based VLMs by an order of magnitude and
achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art specialized and
autoregressive systems. Through block-causal attention and exact
KV-caching, DODO achieves a $`5\times`$ inference speedup over the
autoregressive baseline, establishing discrete diffusion not just as a
theoretical capability, but as a practical, high-performance alternative
for latency-critical applications. Furthermore, we show that the
diffusion framework uniquely enables bidirectional attention across
blocks, which further improves accuracy by pushing the utilizable block
size from $`32`$ to $`256`$ tokens.

</div>

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="section ltx_paragraph">

#### Limitations.

<div id="S7.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">

While DODO significantly accelerates inference, its reliance on exact
KV-caching enforces a static history, limiting accuracy at larger block
sizes compared to the bidirectional variant. Future work will focus on
bridging this gap and exploring diffusion samplers tailored to OCR.

</div>

<div id="A1" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Attention Structure Visualization

<figure id="A1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<img src="2602.16872v2/x7.png" id="A1.F1.g1"
class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="498"
height="278" alt="Refer to caption" />
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A1.F1.3.1.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure A1</span>: </span><span
id="A1.F1.4.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span
id="A1.F1.4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Visualization of the
attention structure.</span> Full bidirectional attention allows prior
blocks to attend to the current block (green hatched), meaning their
internal representations dynamically adapt during the forward pass.
Block-causal masking prevents prior blocks from attending to the current
block. This ensures the history representations remain invariant,
enabling exact KV-caching for faster inference. </span></figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

<div id="A2" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Additional Ablations

<div id="A2.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Sampling Strategies

<figure id="A2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img
src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,"
id="A2.F2.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" /></span>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F2.5.2.1"
class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure B2</span>: </span><span
id="A2.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Edit Distance vs
Speed for different sampling strategies. <span id="A2.F2.2.1.1"
class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Confidence Thresholding (Green)</span>
achieves the optimal balance at <span
class="math inline"><em>p</em> = 0.99</span>, maintaining high accuracy
while offering adaptive speedups.</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

To optimize the inference process, we investigate the impact of the
decoding schedule. Given the intolerance of OCR tasks to transcription
errors, our primary objective is not merely to maximize speed, but to
identify the fastest strategy that maintains high fidelity. We compares
two distinct sampling strategies:

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

- <span id="A2.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Confidence
  Thresholding (Yu et al.,
  <a href="#bib.bib52" class="ltx_ref">2025</a>):</span> A dynamic
  strategy that unmasks all tokens whose prediction probability exceeds
  a fixed threshold $`p`$. This allows for adaptive step sizes: the
  model accelerates through clear text and slows down for ambiguous
  regions. This is the default strategy used in our main experiments
  (with $`p=0.99`$).

  </div>
- <span id="A2.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Confidence
  Top-K (Zheng et al.,
  <a href="#bib.bib54" class="ltx_ref">2023</a>):</span> A fixed-rate
  strategy that unmasks exactly $`K`$ tokens per step, guaranteeing a
  steady generation pace regardless of model confidence.

  </div>

</div>

<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">

Figure <a href="#A2.F2" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure B2 ‣ B.1 Sampling Strategies ‣ Appendix B Additional Ablations ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B2</span></a> illustrates the performance
trade-offs. In the high-accuracy regime required for OCR, Confidence
Thresholding emerges as the superior strategy. By strictly enforcing a
high confidence floor ($`p=0.99`$), it ensures that the model only
commits to tokens when certainty is high. While other strategies (such
as aggressive Top-K) may achieve higher raw throughput, they do so at
the cost of unacceptable error rates. Thus, confidence thresholding
provides the optimal balance, maximizing speed strictly within the
bounds of usable accuracy.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="A3" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Fine-Grained Evaluation Breakdown

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">

We provide a detailed breakdown of OmniDocBench results by document
length and document type.

</div>

<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">

<a href="#A3.T4" class="ltx_ref"
title="In Appendix C Fine-Grained Evaluation Breakdown ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> reveals that DODO’s advantage
over autoregressive VLMs grows with document length: at 4096+ tokens,
DODO achieves $`0.079`$ vs. Qwen 7B’s $`0.185`$, as longer sequences
amplify the benefit of parallel decoding. Conversely, for very short
documents (0–128 tokens), all methods perform similarly since sequential
overhead is minimal.

</div>

<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">

<a href="#A3.T5" class="ltx_ref"
title="In Appendix C Fine-Grained Evaluation Breakdown ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> shows that DODO performs
consistently across document types, with particularly strong results on
PPT slides ($`0.014`$) and academic papers ($`0.050`$). The
bidirectional variant further improves on structured layouts (Academic,
Book) where long-range context aids alignment.

</div>

<div id="A4" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Document Parsing Examples

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">

We present qualitative results in <a href="#A4.F3" class="ltx_ref"
title="In Appendix D Document Parsing Examples ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figures</span> <span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D3</span></a>
and <a href="#A4.F4" class="ltx_ref"
title="Figure D4 ‣ Appendix D Document Parsing Examples ‣ DODO: Discrete OCR Diffusion Models"><span
class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D4</span></a>. Selected from the
OmniDocBench dataset, these examples demonstrate DODO’s capability to
transcribe dense text and preserve complex layout structures, while the
accompanying heatmaps visualize the underlying parallel decoding
process.

</div>

Our team has already identified
<a href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues" class="ltx_ref"

reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your
efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because
disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for
your continued support in championing open access for all.
